extracted.intended_audience: regulated parties, immigration practitioners, legal counsel, policy analysts, and public stakeholders in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards applicable to withdrawing amendatory instructions to a prior final rule (the Security Bars Final Rule), explaining how the Administrative Procedure Act, executive orders, and other statutes apply to this specific regulatory action. Focused on procedural exceptions, good cause, related statutory/regulatory requirements, and the specific regulatory text governing withholding of removal in public-health contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA general notice-and-comment and delayed effective-date requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA generally requires agencies to publish “notice of proposed rule making” in the Federal Register for a period of public comment and generally requires a 30-day delay to the effective date of a rule (5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)-(B); 5 U.S.C. 553(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preamble frames those baseline requirements as the starting point for analysis of exemptions and exceptions discussed below; see also citations to statutory sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment satisfied for this rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Departments concluded this rulemaking satisfies the APA's notice-and-comment requirement because they requested and received public comments during prior delays and sought comment on amendment or rescission in earlier IFRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments considered comments received (including those addressing delay and underlying merits) and relied on prior opportunities for comment as part of the procedural justification for the partial withdrawal now being adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural-rule exception to notice-and-comment and delayed effective-date (housekeeping/procedural rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA's notice-and-comment and delayed-effective-date requirements do not apply to 'rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice' (5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A); 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)). Courts describe the critical feature of such a rule as covering agency actions that do not themselves alter the rights or interests of parties, although it may alter the manner in which parties present themselves or their viewpoints to the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance relies on case law (AFL-CIO v. NLRB; James V. Hurson Assocs. v. Glickman; Neighborhood TV Co. v. FCC; Elec. Priv. Info. Ctr. v. DHS) to explain that courts 'must look at [the rule's] effect on those interests ultimately at stake in the agency proceeding.' An otherwise-procedural rule does not become substantive simply because it imposes burdens; a 'housekeeping' measure that does not alter eligibility or rights falls within the procedural exception. The Departments determined withdrawing identified amendatory instructions is procedural (housekeeping) because it will not alter individuals' rights or eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception to notice-and-comment and delayed effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may for 'good cause' find that notice and public procedure is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest and may forgo a delayed effective date for 'good cause found' (5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B); 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When finding notice-and-comment 'unnecessary,' agencies should consider whether the rule is 'insignificant in nature and impact' or 'minor or merely technical' (Util. Solid Waste Activities Grp.; North Carolina Growers' Ass'n; Nat'l Nutritional Foods Ass'n). The Departments conclude notice-and-comment is unnecessary here because intervening rules adopted after the Security Bars Final Rule reversed or altered the substantive policy choices in the amendatory instructions, making withdrawal a technical change to avoid codifying confusing or conflicting text. For delayed effective date, courts ask whether immediate implementation outweighs parties' need to prepare (Riverbend Farms; Am. Fed'n of Gov't Emps. v. Block); here regulated parties were on notice and no preparation time is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign affairs exception to APA requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 U.S.C. 553 does not apply when a rule involves a 'foreign affairs function of the United States' (5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)). Courts have applied this exception when a rule 'clearly and directly involves a foreign affairs function,' and some courts require a showing that notice/comment would lead to 'definitely undesirable international consequences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments assert the rule satisfies both standards because it is intended to ensure continued ability to process aliens using expedited removal and to avoid interrupting removal processes that could harm foreign policy objectives (citations: E.B. v. U.S. Dep't of State; Rajah v. Mukasey; Determination: Foreign Affairs Functions of the United States). The preamble links rule implementation to foreign negotiations, travel-document issuance, removal cooperation, and other international consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866/13563 analytical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 12866 and EO 13563 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select approaches that maximize net benefits; EO 13563 emphasizes quantifying costs and benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this rule is not economically significant under EO 12866 section 3(f)(1), OMB designated it a 'significant regulatory action' under section 3(f) and reviewed the rule. EO 14192's special offset requirement (eliminate costs from at least 10 prior regulations) is noted but the Departments state the rule is not subject to EO 14192 because it concerns immigration functions; OMB memorandum cited for implementation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act applicability and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires agencies to prepare and make available a regulatory flexibility analysis describing effects on small entities when a rule is subject to notice of proposed rulemaking (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments determined the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it regulates individuals (aliens), not small entities as defined in 5 U.S.C. 601(6). Also, RFA analysis requirements apply only to rules requiring publication of a general notice of proposed rulemaking; because Departments permissibly forwent notice-and-comment for the reasons given, an RFA analysis was not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: UMRA requires agencies to prepare a written statement assessing effects of any Federal mandate that may result in expenditures of $100 million or more in any one year by State, local, and Tribal governments or the private sector (2 U.S.C. 1532(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments concluded the final rule does not contain a Federal mandate as defined under UMRA (no enforceable duty on State/local/Tribal governments or private sector), so UMRA's Title II requirements and statement are not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act (major rule) determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Congressional Review Act (Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996), a rule is a 'major rule' if it results in annual economic effects of $100 million or more or other specified major effects (5 U.S.C. 804(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs determined this rule is not a 'major rule' as defined by section 804 and will not have the threshold economic effects or substantial adverse impacts described in the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13132 (Federalism) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13132 requires analysis of substantial direct effects on the States or federal-state relationships that would warrant a federalism summary impact statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments concluded this final rule does not have substantial direct effects on the States, the relationship between national and state governments, or on distribution of power and responsibilities, and therefore a federalism summary impact statement is not warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 12988 sets standards to reduce litigation and ensure clarity/consistency in regulations (sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments state that this rule meets the applicable standards set forth in EO 12988 sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13175 (Tribal consultation) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13175 requires consultation and coordination with Indian Tribal governments when a rule has tribal implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments determined the rule does not have Tribal implications because it would not have substantial direct effect on Indian Tribes, relationships with the Federal Government, or distribution of power/responsibilities; therefore EO 13175 does not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA categorical exclusion criteria (DHS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be categorically excluded it must satisfy three conditions: (1) the entire action clearly fits within one or more categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the potential for a significant environmental effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS determined this rule fits within categorical exclusion A3 because it is an administrative change with no change in environmental effect, is not part of a larger Federal action, and presents no extraordinary circumstances. DOJ adopted DHS's categorical exclusion determination under 42 U.S.C. 4336c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Paperwork Reduction Act governs 'collections of information' and requires OMB review of new or revised collections (44 U.S.C. chapter 35; 5 CFR part 1320).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments state this rule does not adopt new or revise existing collections of information as defined by the PRA, and thus PRA requirements are not triggered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housekeeping nature of withdrawing amendatory instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawing identified amendatory instructions will not alter individuals' rights or interests, nor alter eligibility requirements for relief or protection from removal, nor place new substantive burdens on regulated parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because withdrawal prevents codifying confusing or conflicting regulatory text and avoids writing over later-adopted regulatory amendments, the Departments treat this action as a technical/housekeeping change that preserves the substance of the Security Bars Final Rule and falls within procedural exceptions to APA requirements (citing Elec. Priv. Info. Ctr.; JEM Broad. Co.; James V. Hurson Assocs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding of removal — mandatory denial general rule and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as provided in paragraph (d)(3), an application for withholding of removal under section 241(b)(3) or under CAT regulations shall be denied if the applicant falls within section 241(b)(3)(B) (or prior section 243(h)(2) for certain older proceedings). If evidence indicates applicability of one or more statutory grounds for denial of withholding, the applicant bears the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that such grounds do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates the regulatory framework for 'mandatory denials' of withholding and clarifies evidentiary burden in adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding of removal — public health emergencies criterion (symptoms/contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a communicable disease has triggered an ongoing declaration of a public health emergency under Federal law (e.g., PHS Act §319 or FD&C Act §564), then an alien is ineligible for withholding of removal on the basis of being a danger to the security of the United States if the alien (A) exhibits symptoms indicating affliction with the disease (per guidance issued by the Secretary or the Attorney General), or (B) has come into contact with the disease within the number of days equivalent to the longest known incubation and contagion period for the disease (per guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule ties eligibility to public-health emergency declarations and to operational guidance from the Secretary or Attorney General on symptoms, incubation/contagion periods, and contact definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding of removal — danger to public health caused by epidemic outside the United States (joint determination and designation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a communicable disease of public health significance (42 CFR 34.2(b)), if the Secretary and the Attorney General, in consultation with the HHS Secretary, jointly determine that physical presence in the U.S. of aliens coming from designated countries/places (or who embarked at designated places during specified periods) would cause a danger to the public health and they designate the country/place/time/circumstances and any exceptions, then those aliens or classes are ineligible for withholding of removal under section 241(b)(3)(B)(iv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicability requires a joint determination and designation (with consultation), and the Departments may include exceptions as appropriate; the provision operationalizes exclusion based on origin/place/time tied to epidemic prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for Canada-return applicants under Canada Cooperation Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The grounds for mandatory denial described for public health emergencies and epidemics shall not apply to an alien who is applying for asylum or withholding of removal in the United States upon return from Canada and pursuant to the Agreement Between the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada for Cooperation in the Examination of Refugee Status Claims from Nationals of Third Countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies an explicit statutory/regulatory exception preserving eligibility for applicants covered by the U.S.-Canada cooperation agreement.
